Muktikopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a well-known minor Upaniṣad assigned to the Śukla Yajurveda. It is often referred to by others since it gives a long list of 108 उपनिषद्स्. It is in two adhyāyas or chapters containing 134 mantras mostly in the anuṣṭubh metre, the rest being in prose.
It is cast in the form of a dialogue between हनुमान् and Śrī राम the emperor, (considered as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु Himself) at अयोध्या, the capital from where he ruled.
Hanumān asks Śrī राम as to his greatness and the way of attaining लिबेरतिओन् without much effort. Śrī राम replies that by the true knowledge of Vedānta, one can get the मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् known as सायुज्य, absorption into him. Incidentally he gives the several divisions of the वेदस् (which are produced by his breath as it were) and the उपनिषद्स्.
In answer to another question by हनुमान् about the various descriptions of मुक्ति given by others, Śrī राम delineates four kinds of mukti—sālokya (attaining his world), सामीप्य (living near him), sārūpya (having a form similar to his) and सायुज्य (unity in him)—and praises the greatness of the तारकमन्त्र (‘Rāma’) uttered by शिव, the Lord of काशी, in the ears of persons dying there.
However, he also stresses that only a knowledge of the उपनिषद्स् can give लिबेरतिओन्. Then he proceeds to give the names of 108 उपनिषद्स्. (All these are now available in print, with the commentary of Upaniṣadbrahma Yogīndra.)
Then comes the method of giving the knowledge of these उपनिषद्स् to worthy seekers. Atheists, ungrateful ones, persons of evil character, those who lack devotion to God, those who have no love for the guru—all these are unfit to receive this knowledge. On the other hand, the disciples devoted to the service of the गुरु, those who are of good character and devoted to God should be given this knowledge after testing them.
Next, there is a long section giving the शान्तिमन्त्रस् (peace-invocations) for the various उपनिषद्स्. They are decided as per the Veda to which the Upaniṣad belongs: vāṅ me manasi for the उपनिषद्स् of the Ṛgveda (like Aitareya and Kauṣītaki); pūrṇamadaḥ for the उपनिषद्स् of the Śukla Yajurveda (like Īśāvāsya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka); saha nā vavatu for the उपनिषद्स् of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (like Kaṭha and Taittirīya); āpyāyantu for the उपनिषद्स् of the Sāmaveda (like Kena and Chāndogya); bhadraṁ karṇebhiḥ for the उपनिषद्स् of the Atharvaṇaveda (like Praśna and Muṇḍaka).
Here ends the first chapter.
The Second chapter deals mainly with जीवन्मुक्ति (liberation while living in the body) and videhamukti (liberation from future transmigration after death).
It is the vāsanās (tendencies and impressions in the मिन्द् carried over from previous lives) that are responsible for bondage. Hence, in order to get लिबेरतिओन्, the seeker has to practise simultaneously विज्ञान (knowledge about the आत्मन् or the true Self), vāsanākṣaya (attenuation and destruction of the vāsanās) and manonāśa (destruction of the tendencies in the मिन्द् that arise involuntarily).
The Upaniṣad then proceeds to des-cribe in detail how they can be achieved. Desisting from the will to fulfil desires, practising प्राणायाम and meditating on pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् as the essence behind one’s Self and the world—these are the means of attaining जीवन्मुक्ति.
See also JĪVANMUKTI-VIVEKA.

muktapuruṣa
(‘the liberated person’)
------------------------------------------
The basic works of हिन्दुइस्म् like the उपनिषद्स् and the Bhagavadgītā, as also several secondary treatises based on them like the epics and the पुराणस्, have described in detail, the characteristics of a मुक्तपुरुष, the liberated person, also called ‘jīvanmukta’ (‘liberated even while living in the body’).
The आत्मन् or the सोउल् (the Self) is essentially free. But, that he has got himself entangled in the body-मिन्द् complex, that he is therefore suffering much and that he is undergoing transmigration repeatedly, is also a recognised fact. Though the cause of his bondage and the means of his deliverance as described in the various philosophical systems of हिन्दुइस्म् may appear to differ, descriptions of his state of लिबेरतिओन् are, more or less similar. The Kaṭhopaniṣad (5.1) says that a मुक्तपुरुष is fully free from all kinds of desires. So does the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.4.7). Some of the other उपनिषद्स् declare that a liberated सोउल् is absolutely untouched by any kind of sin, heinous or venial (vide Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇopaniṣad 3.1).
Excellent and detailed descriptions of a मुक्तपुरुष, called variously ‘jīvanmukta,’ ‘sthitaprajña,’ ‘bhakta,’ ‘guṇātīta,’ ‘brāhmaṇa’ and ‘ativarṇāśrami’ are found in a number of authoritative religious works like Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha (5th sarga), Bhagavadgītā (2.54-64; 12.13-19; 14.21-26), Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva 245.12-24) and Sūtasaṁhitā (Muktikhaṇḍa 5.9-42).
The gist of all these descriptions is that his मिन्द् has transcended all pairs of opposites like happiness and misery, likes and dislikes as also the various passions and prejudices like lust and greed, avarice and delusion, pride, vanity and jealousy. He is ever immersed in the bliss of the आत्मन् inside and looks upon the world as a reflection or a manifestation of ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute.
See also BANDHA and MOKṢA.

mukuṭa
(‘that which decorates [the head]’)
------------------------------------------
Mukuṭa (also spelt as ‘makuṭa’) is headwear or crown. In iconographical works, almost all the images—whether of gods or semi-gods or demons or human beings—are shown with some kind of मुकुट.
There are varieties of the same. Some of them are:
kirīṭamukuṭa—It is a crown, usually 16 to 24 aṅgulas in height and cylindrical or conical in shape with details like a diadem or a lotus or studded with gems. It is shown on the heads of male deities like विष्णु as also emperors. Sometimes देवी images too have them.
karaṇḍamukuṭa—shaped like a pot or a bulb, it is shown as adorning the major feminine deities and also kings. The lower part of this crown may be studded with precious stones.
jaṭāmukuṭa—Here, the matted hair is done up like a crown. This is generally shown in the images of शिव, his attendants as also the sages and in some forms of the देवी.
In the images of yakṣas and the नागस्, a turban-like headgear, called śirastraka, is provided.

Muktābāī
------------------------------------------
Sant Jñāneśvar (A. D. 1275-1296) was the earliest of the saints of Maharashtra who initiated the भक्ति Movement. His elder brother Nivṛttinātha (a disciple of Gayanīnātha, a follower of the नाथ चुल्त्) was his गुरु. Sopāna was his younger brother and मुक्ताबाई, his sister, the youngest in the family.
Muktā, as she was fondly known, was considered as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of महामाया (the power of Lord विष्णु). She too was a highly evolved saint and was the spiritual teacher of Visobā Khecar and Cāṅgadev (a great haṭhayogi, well-known for his psychic powers).
There are a few अभङ्गस् (bhajans in Marāṭhi) in her name.
See also JÑĀNEŚVARA.
